html:
A Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe that sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 without a compass or any instruments, proving that ancient Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate navigation.

Some scholars had argued that the far islands of Polynesia were reached by accident, by canoes drifting off course. To test this, the Polynesian Voyaging Society, founded in 1973, built a replica of an ancient canoe and launched it in 1975. No Hawaiian still knew the old way of finding land at sea, so the crew turned to Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia.

Mau steered by the rising and setting points of stars, the shape of swells, the flight of birds and the colour of the sky. After about a month at sea the canoe reached Tahiti.

The voyage helped spark a revival of Hawaiian culture and pride. Nainoa Thompson learned from Mau and became the first Hawaiian in centuries to navigate this way. The canoe has since sailed around the world, following the route of the settlement of East Polynesia and of navigators like Tupaia.
sum: A Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe that sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 without a compass or any instruments, proving that ancient Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate navigation.
